Week 14 · Phase 4: Advanced Topics

Graph Neural Networks and Geometric Deep Learning

Learning on graphs and other structured domains. Graph data and tasks, adjacency, degree and Laplacian matrices, the message-passing framework, GCN (with a derivation of normalized propagation and its spectral motivation), GraphSAGE, GAT and GIN, expressive power and the Weisfeiler-Lehman test, over-smoothing and over-squashing with their remedies, pooling and readout, node, link and graph tasks, graph Transformers, and the geometric deep learning blueprint (symmetry, invariance, equivariance) with point clouds, PointNet and equivariant networks. The lab uses PyTorch Geometric on Cora and a molecular dataset.

98 min read3 interactive demos13 figures32 code blocks10 exercises
Learning objectives

By the end of this week you should be able to:

  • Describe how molecules, social networks, knowledge graphs and recommender systems are represented as graphs, and name the node-, edge- and graph-level tasks defined on them.
  • Build the adjacency, degree and Laplacian matrices of a graph, and explain what the Laplacian quadratic form and its eigenvectors measure.
  • State the message-passing framework (message, aggregate, update, readout) and prove that it is permutation equivariant.
  • Derive the GCN propagation rule A^=D~−1/2(A+I)D~−1/2\hat{\mathbf A}=\tilde{\mathbf D}^{-1/2}(\mathbf A+\mathbf I)\tilde{\mathbf D}^{-1/2}A^=D~−1/2(A+I)D~−1/2 from a first-order spectral filter and the renormalization trick, and compare it with GraphSAGE, GAT and GIN.
  • State precisely what the 1-Weisfeiler-Lehman (1-WL) test is, what message-passing GNNs can and cannot distinguish, and why GIN uses sum aggregation and an MLP.
  • Explain over-smoothing (with a Dirichlet-energy argument) and over-squashing (with a receptive-field argument), and list remedies: residual and initial connections, normalization, DropEdge, jumping knowledge, rewiring, and virtual nodes.
  • Choose a readout or pooling operator (sum, mean, max, attention, hierarchical) and say what each one can and cannot count.
  • Explain how graph Transformers use positional and structural encodings to inject graph structure into full attention.
  • State the geometric deep learning blueprint in terms of groups, invariance and equivariance, and identify the symmetry behind CNNs, GNNs, DeepSets and PointNet.
  • Implement PointNet and an E(n)-equivariant layer, and verify invariance and equivariance numerically.
  • Train GNNs with PyTorch Geometric for node classification on Cora and graph classification on a molecular dataset.

Everything you have built so far assumed a regular layout. A CNN (Week 5) needs pixels on a grid, an RNN or Transformer (Week 7, Week 9) needs tokens in a line. Much of the interesting data in science and industry has no such layout. A molecule is a set of atoms joined by bonds; there is no "left" or "up" in it. A social network is a set of people and friendships. A road network, a protein interaction map, the citation record of a research field, the purchase history of a million shoppers: all of these are graphs, where the objects matter and the relations between them matter equally.

A graph neural network (GNN) is a neural network designed so that its computation respects the structure of a graph. The central design constraint is easy to state and surprisingly deep. There is no canonical order of the nodes, so the network must give the same answer however you number them. That single requirement, permutation symmetry, forces the architecture: each node updates itself by pooling over its neighbours with an order-independent function, and this local operation is repeated layer after layer. This is message passing.

This week has two halves. The first half builds the graph-learning toolbox: representations, message passing, the four workhorse layers (GCN, GraphSAGE, GAT, GIN), a rigorous look at what such networks can and cannot compute, why deep GNNs misbehave, how to turn node embeddings into graph-level predictions, and where Transformers fit. The second half zooms out. Permutation invariance is one example of a general principle, and CNNs, GNNs, DeepSets and equivariant 3-D networks are all instances of the same geometric deep learning blueprint: choose the symmetry group of your domain and build layers that commute with it. The lab uses PyTorch Geometric (PyG) on a citation network and on a molecular dataset.

Graph-structured data

A graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E)G=(V,E) consists of a set of nodes (vertices) VVV with ∣V∣=n|V|=n∣V∣=n and a set of edges E⊆V×VE\subseteq V\times VE⊆V×V. Each node vvv may carry a feature vector xv∈Rd\boldsymbol{x}_v\in\R^{d}xv​∈Rd, each edge (u,v)(u,v)(u,v) may carry a feature vector euv\boldsymbol{e}_{uv}euv​, and the whole graph may carry a label or target. Edges can be undirected or directed, weighted or unweighted. A graph can also have several types of nodes and edges (a heterogeneous graph). Before touching any math, look at how four very different domains map onto this one abstraction.

Molecules. Nodes are atoms, edges are covalent bonds. Node features encode the element (one-hot over C, N, O, ...), formal charge, hybridization or aromaticity; edge features encode the bond type (single, double, triple, aromatic). The typical task is graph-level regression or classification: predict a property of the whole molecule such as solubility, toxicity, binding affinity or an energy. A typical drug-like molecule has 20 to 50 heavy atoms, so the graphs are small, but there are millions of them. Molecular graphs are also sparse (an atom has at most about four bonds) and planar-ish, and the identity of a molecule is the graph itself, independent of how the atoms are numbered in a file. This is the setting where the invariance requirement is most obvious: a toxicity predictor that depends on atom numbering is simply wrong.

Social and information networks. Nodes are users, papers or web pages; edges are friendships, citations or hyperlinks. These graphs can be enormous (billions of edges), have heavy-tailed degree distributions (a few hubs with millions of neighbours), and usually come with sparse labels. Typical tasks are node classification (which research area is this paper in? is this account a bot?) and link prediction (who will this user befriend?). Most of this graph is unlabeled, which is why semi-supervised learning, where the structure itself spreads information from the few labeled nodes, is the classic setup.

Knowledge graphs. Nodes are entities (Marie Curie, Warsaw, physics) and edges are typed relations (born_in, field_of). The data is a set of triples (h,r,t)(h, r, t)(h,r,t). Typical tasks are link prediction (complete the missing triple: is (Curie,born_in,?)(\text{Curie}, \text{born\_in}, ?)(Curie,born_in,?) answerable?) and entity classification. The typed edges mean a plain GNN is not enough; Relational GCN (R-GCN, Schlichtkrull et al., 2018) gives every relation its own weight matrix.

Recommender systems. Users and items form a bipartite graph whose edges are interactions (clicks, purchases, ratings). Recommendation is link prediction on this graph: which unobserved user-item edge is most likely? GNN-based recommenders (PinSage at Pinterest, 2018; LightGCN, 2020) learn user and item embeddings by propagating over the interaction graph, so that two items bought by overlapping sets of users end up close together.

Other domains follow the same pattern: proteins (residues as nodes, contacts as edges), road networks (intersections and segments, used for traffic and arrival-time prediction), physical simulation (particles or mesh vertices with interactions), circuits, code (abstract syntax trees and data-flow graphs), and scene graphs of images. What these have in common is that the relational structure is part of the input, of variable size, and has no natural ordering.

Why not just flatten the graph?

The obvious baseline is to flatten the adjacency matrix and feed it to an MLP. It fails for three independent reasons. First, graphs have variable size, while an MLP has a fixed input width. Second, the matrix depends on an arbitrary node ordering: the same graph has up to n!n!n! different adjacency matrices, and an MLP would have to learn all of them separately. Third, an n×nn\times nn×n input has O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) entries even when the graph has only O(n)O(n)O(n) edges. We want a model whose parameters do not depend on nnn, whose output does not depend on the ordering, and whose cost scales with the number of edges. GNNs satisfy all three.

History

A short history. Neural networks on graphs go back to Gori, Monfardini and Scarselli (2005) and the "graph neural network model" of Scarselli et al. (2009), which iterated a recurrent update to a fixed point. Convolutions on graphs came from the spectral side (Bruna et al., 2014; Defferrard et al., 2016, using Chebyshev polynomials). The pivotal simplification was Kipf and Welling's GCN in 2017, a two-line propagation rule that worked remarkably well on citation graphs. In the same year Hamilton et al. introduced GraphSAGE for inductive learning on large graphs, and Gilmer et al. unified many models as "message passing neural networks" for quantum chemistry. Velickovic et al. added attention in 2018 (GAT), Xu et al. tied GNN power to the Weisfeiler-Lehman test in 2019 (GIN), and the 2021 monograph by Bronstein, Bruna, Cohen and Velickovic placed all of this inside "geometric deep learning".

Graph basics: adjacency, degree and the Laplacian

Number the nodes 1,…,n1,\dots,n1,…,n. The adjacency matrix A∈{0,1}n×n\mathbf A\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}A∈{0,1}n×n has Aij=1A_{ij}=1Aij​=1 if there is an edge from iii to jjj. For an undirected graph A\mathbf AA is symmetric. The degree of a node is its number of neighbours, di=∑jAijd_i=\sum_j A_{ij}di​=∑j​Aij​, and the degree matrix is D=diag⁡(d1,…,dn)\mathbf D=\diag(d_1,\dots,d_n)D=diag(d1​,…,dn​). Stack node features into X∈Rn×d\mathbf X\in\R^{n\times d}X∈Rn×d, whose row iii is xi⊤\boldsymbol{x}_i^\topxi⊤​.

Multiplying by A\mathbf AA is the fundamental graph operation. For a feature matrix X\mathbf XX,

(AX)i=∑jAij xj=∑j∈N(i)xj,(\mathbf A\mathbf X)_{i}=\sum_{j}A_{ij}\,\boldsymbol{x}_j=\sum_{j\in\mathcal N(i)}\boldsymbol{x}_j ,(AX)i​=j∑​Aij​xj​=j∈N(i)∑​xj​,

which is the sum of the features of the neighbours of node iii. One matrix product aggregates every neighbourhood simultaneously. Likewise D−1AX\mathbf D^{-1}\mathbf A\mathbf XD−1AX is the neighbour mean, and Ak\mathbf A^kAk counts walks of length kkk: (Ak)ij(\mathbf A^k)_{ij}(Ak)ij​ is the number of walks from iii to jjj with exactly kkk edges. So a kkk-layer network that multiplies by A\mathbf AA at each layer mixes information within kkk hops. Keep this in mind; it is the reason depth equals receptive-field radius in a GNN.

The graph Laplacian

The combinatorial Laplacian is L=D−A\mathbf L=\mathbf D-\mathbf AL=D−A and the symmetric normalized Laplacian is

Lsym=I−D−1/2A D−1/2.\mathbf L_{\mathrm{sym}}=\mathbf I-\mathbf D^{-1/2}\mathbf A\,\mathbf D^{-1/2}.Lsym​=I−D−1/2AD−1/2.

The Laplacian is the graph analogue of the second derivative, and its quadratic form measures how rough a signal is. Let x∈Rn\boldsymbol{x}\in\R^nx∈Rn assign one scalar to each node. Then

x⊤L x=∑idixi2−∑i,jAijxixj=12∑i,jAij(xi−xj)2=∑(i,j)∈E(xi−xj)2.\boldsymbol{x}^\top\mathbf L\,\boldsymbol{x}=\sum_i d_i x_i^2-\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}x_ix_j=\frac12\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}(x_i-x_j)^2=\sum_{(i,j)\in E}(x_i-x_j)^2 .x⊤Lx=i∑​di​xi2​−i,j∑​Aij​xi​xj​=21​i,j∑​Aij​(xi​−xj​)2=(i,j)∈E∑​(xi​−xj​)2.

(The middle step expands the square and uses ∑jAij=di\sum_j A_{ij}=d_i∑j​Aij​=di​; the last sums each undirected edge once.) This Dirichlet energy is zero exactly when x\boldsymbol{x}x is constant on every connected component, and it is large when neighbouring nodes disagree. So the Laplacian measures smoothness over the graph. Three facts about its spectrum matter for GNNs:

  • L\mathbf LL is symmetric positive semi-definite, so it has real eigenvalues 0=λ1≤λ2≤⋯≤λn0=\lambda_1\le\lambda_2\le\dots\le\lambda_n0=λ1​≤λ2​≤⋯≤λn​ and orthonormal eigenvectors.
  • The multiplicity of the eigenvalue 000 equals the number of connected components. The eigenvector for a connected graph is the constant vector.
  • Eigenvectors with small eigenvalues vary slowly over the graph ("low frequency") and those with large eigenvalues oscillate between neighbours ("high frequency"), exactly like sines and cosines of increasing frequency. The eigenvalues of Lsym\mathbf L_{\mathrm{sym}}Lsym​ lie in [0,2][0,2][0,2].

The second eigenvector (the Fiedler vector) is the smoothest non-constant signal and is the basis of spectral clustering: its sign pattern splits the graph into two clusters with few edges between them. The code below builds all of these on a toy graph made of two triangles joined by a bridge.

pythongraph_basics.py
import numpy as np

# a small graph: two triangles joined by a bridge (nodes 0-2 and 3-5)
edges = [(0, 1), (1, 2), (0, 2), (3, 4), (4, 5), (3, 5), (2, 3)]
n = 6
A = np.zeros((n, n))
for u, v in edges:
    A[u, v] = A[v, u] = 1.0            # undirected: symmetric adjacency

deg = A.sum(axis=1)                    # degrees d_i = sum_j A_ij
D = np.diag(deg)
L = D - A                              # combinatorial Laplacian
L_sym = np.eye(n) - np.diag(deg**-0.5) @ A @ np.diag(deg**-0.5)   # normalized Laplacian

print("degrees:", deg)
evals, evecs = np.linalg.eigh(L_sym)
print("eigenvalues of L_sym:", np.round(evals, 3))

# Dirichlet energy x^T L x = sum over edges (x_u - x_v)^2
x = np.array([1., 1., 1., -1., -1., -1.])
print("x^T L x =", x @ L @ x, " edge-sum =", sum((x[u]-x[v])**2 for u, v in edges))

# Fiedler vector of L: sign pattern recovers the two clusters (up to a global sign)
w, V = np.linalg.eigh(L)
print("Fiedler vector signs:", np.sign(V[:, 1]).astype(int))
text
degrees: [2. 2. 3. 3. 2. 2.]
eigenvalues of L_sym: [-0.     0.205  1.167  1.5    1.5    1.629]
x^T L x = 4.0  edge-sum = 4.0
Fiedler vector signs: [-1 -1 -1  1  1  1]

The signal that is +1+1+1 on one triangle and −1-1−1 on the other has energy 444: only the bridge edge contributes, and it contributes (1−(−1))2=4(1-(-1))^2=4(1−(−1))2=4. The single eigenvalue 000 confirms one connected component, and the tiny second eigenvalue 0.2050.2050.205 says the graph is nearly disconnected (there is a bottleneck). Remember this bottleneck picture; it comes back as over-squashing.

Permutations and the symmetry we need

Relabelling nodes with a permutation π\piπ is represented by a permutation matrix P\mathbf PP (exactly one 111 per row and column). The relabelled graph has adjacency PAP⊤\mathbf P\mathbf A\mathbf P^\topPAP⊤ and features PX\mathbf P\mathbf XPX. Any sensible model fff must treat (A,X)(\mathbf A,\mathbf X)(A,X) and (PAP⊤,PX)(\mathbf P\mathbf A\mathbf P^\top,\mathbf P\mathbf X)(PAP⊤,PX) as the same graph. For node-level outputs this means the outputs get permuted along with the nodes (equivariance); for graph-level outputs the output must not change at all (invariance):

f(PAP⊤,PX)=Pf(A,X)(equivariant),g(PAP⊤,PX)=g(A,X)(invariant).f(\mathbf P\mathbf A\mathbf P^\top,\mathbf P\mathbf X)=\mathbf P f(\mathbf A,\mathbf X)\quad\text{(equivariant)},\qquad g(\mathbf P\mathbf A\mathbf P^\top,\mathbf P\mathbf X)=g(\mathbf A,\mathbf X)\quad\text{(invariant)}.f(PAP⊤,PX)=Pf(A,X)(equivariant),g(PAP⊤,PX)=g(A,X)(invariant).

We will make these precise and general in the geometric deep learning section. For now, every layer we design must satisfy the first identity, and the final readout must satisfy the second.

The message-passing framework

Here is the idea of a GNN in one sentence: every node repeatedly collects information from its neighbours and updates its own representation. Let hv(0)=xv\boldsymbol{h}_v^{(0)}=\boldsymbol{x}_vhv(0)​=xv​. One layer of message passing computes, for every node vvv,

av(ℓ)=AGGREGATE⁡(ℓ)({ ⁣ ⁣{ MESSAGE⁡(ℓ)(hu(ℓ−1),hv(ℓ−1),euv) : u∈N(v) } ⁣ ⁣}),hv(ℓ)=UPDATE⁡(ℓ)(hv(ℓ−1),av(ℓ)).\boldsymbol{a}_v^{(\ell)}=\operatorname{AGGREGATE}^{(\ell)}\Big(\big\{\!\!\big\{\ \operatorname{MESSAGE}^{(\ell)}\big(\boldsymbol{h}_u^{(\ell-1)},\boldsymbol{h}_v^{(\ell-1)},\boldsymbol{e}_{uv}\big)\ :\ u\in\mathcal N(v)\ \big\}\!\!\big\}\Big), \qquad \boldsymbol{h}_v^{(\ell)}=\operatorname{UPDATE}^{(\ell)}\big(\boldsymbol{h}_v^{(\ell-1)},\boldsymbol{a}_v^{(\ell)}\big).av(ℓ)​=AGGREGATE(ℓ)({{ MESSAGE(ℓ)(hu(ℓ−1)​,hv(ℓ−1)​,euv​) : u∈N(v) }}),hv(ℓ)​=UPDATE(ℓ)(hv(ℓ−1)​,av(ℓ)​).

The double braces denote a multiset (neighbours can repeat a value, and order is meaningless). Three ingredients:

  1. MESSAGE turns a neighbour's state (optionally with the receiver's state and the edge features) into a message vector. It is often just a linear map Whu\mathbf W\boldsymbol{h}_uWhu​.
  2. AGGREGATE combines a variable number of messages into one fixed-size vector. It must be permutation invariant: sum, mean, max, or a learned but symmetric function. This is where the symmetry is enforced.
  3. UPDATE merges the aggregated message with the node's own previous state, typically with an MLP and a nonlinearity.

After LLL layers, the final node embeddings hv(L)\boldsymbol{h}_v^{(L)}hv(L)​ feed a task head: a linear classifier for node classification, a dot-product or MLP over a pair of embeddings for link prediction, or a readout that pools all nodes for graph-level prediction,

hG=READOUT⁡({ ⁣ ⁣{hv(L):v∈V} ⁣ ⁣}).\boldsymbol{h}_G=\operatorname{READOUT}\big(\{\!\!\{\boldsymbol{h}_v^{(L)}:v\in V\}\!\!\}\big).hG​=READOUT({{hv(L)​:v∈V}}).

This template was named the message passing neural network (MPNN) by Gilmer, Schoenholz, Riley, Vinyals and Dahl (2017, ICML), who used it for predicting quantum-chemical properties of molecules, and it subsumes nearly every layer in the rest of this section.

Receptive fields: depth equals hops

After one layer, hv(1)\boldsymbol{h}_v^{(1)}hv(1)​ depends on vvv and its immediate neighbours. After two layers it depends on the 2-hop neighbourhood, because the neighbours' states already contained their neighbours. In general, hv(L)\boldsymbol{h}_v^{(L)}hv(L)​ is a function of exactly the nodes within distance LLL of vvv (the computation tree of depth LLL rooted at vvv). Information cannot travel faster than one hop per layer. Two consequences follow immediately. A shallow GNN is blind to anything farther than LLL hops. And to let two distant nodes interact you need depth at least equal to their distance, which, as we will see, is exactly where trouble starts.

The first demo lets you watch this happen. Put a one-hot signal at node 0 and press Step: after kkk layers the signal has reached exactly the nodes within kkk hops, and the numbers show how each aggregator rescales it.

Why this respects permutation symmetry

Proposition: message passing layers are permutation equivariant

Suppose AGGREGATE is permutation invariant (it depends on the multiset of messages only) and MESSAGE and UPDATE are applied identically at every node (shared weights). Let π\piπ be a relabelling of the nodes. Then the output at node π(v)\pi(v)π(v) of the relabelled graph equals the output at node vvv of the original graph.

Proof sketch. Induct on the layer. At layer 000 the states are the (relabelled) features. Assume layer ℓ−1\ell-1ℓ−1 is equivariant. The neighbours of π(v)\pi(v)π(v) in the relabelled graph are exactly π(u)\pi(u)π(u) for u∈N(v)u\in\mathcal N(v)u∈N(v), with the same edge features, and by hypothesis their states equal the original states hu(ℓ−1)\boldsymbol{h}_u^{(\ell-1)}hu(ℓ−1)​. The multiset of messages arriving at π(v)\pi(v)π(v) is therefore the same multiset that arrived at vvv, so the (order-independent) aggregate is the same, and so is the update. □\square□

The NumPy check below verifies this on a six-node graph, and shows what goes wrong if you mix node positions with a generic matrix.

pythonmp_equivariance.py
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, d_in, d_out = 6, 4, 3
A = np.zeros((n, n))
for u, v in [(0, 1), (1, 2), (0, 2), (3, 4), (4, 5), (3, 5), (2, 3)]:
    A[u, v] = A[v, u] = 1.0
X = rng.normal(size=(n, d_in))
W_self, W_nb = rng.normal(size=(d_in, d_out)), rng.normal(size=(d_in, d_out))

def mp_layer(A, X):
    """h_v' = relu(W_self h_v + W_nb * sum_{u in N(v)} h_u), all nodes at once."""
    return np.maximum(0, X @ W_self + (A @ X) @ W_nb)

H = mp_layer(A, X)
print("output shape:", H.shape)

# permutation equivariance: relabel the nodes with permutation matrix P
perm = rng.permutation(n)
P = np.eye(n)[perm]                    # (P X)[i] = X[perm[i]]
H_perm = mp_layer(P @ A @ P.T, P @ X)
print("equivariant:", np.allclose(H_perm, P @ H))

# a readout (sum over nodes) is permutation INVARIANT
print("invariant readout:", np.allclose(H_perm.sum(0), H.sum(0)))

# a layer that mixes node positions is NOT equivariant
W_bad = rng.normal(size=(n, n))
f_bad = lambda X: W_bad @ X
print("position-mixing MLP equivariant:", np.allclose(f_bad(P @ X), P @ f_bad(X)))
text
output shape: (6, 3)
equivariant: True
invariant readout: True
position-mixing MLP equivariant: False
Edge-wise implementation

Real libraries never build the dense n×nn\times nn×n matrix. They store the graph as an edge index of shape 2×∣E∣2\times|E|2×∣E∣ (source and target node of each directed edge), compute one message per edge by gathering source features, and scatter-add the messages into target nodes. This costs O(∣E∣ d)O(|E|\,d)O(∣E∣d) time and memory instead of O(n2d)O(n^2 d)O(n2d). An undirected edge is stored as two directed edges. PyTorch Geometric's MessagePassing base class implements exactly this gather, message, scatter-aggregate, update pipeline.

Graph convolutional networks (GCN)

The graph convolutional network of Kipf and Welling (2017, ICLR, "Semi-supervised classification with graph convolutional networks") is the simplest effective message-passing layer. In matrix form, one layer is

H(ℓ)=σ ⁣(A^ H(ℓ−1) W(ℓ)),A^=D~−1/2A~ D~−1/2,A~=A+I,D~ii=∑jA~ij.\mathbf H^{(\ell)}=\sigma\!\Big(\hat{\mathbf A}\,\mathbf H^{(\ell-1)}\,\mathbf W^{(\ell)}\Big),\qquad \hat{\mathbf A}=\tilde{\mathbf D}^{-1/2}\tilde{\mathbf A}\,\tilde{\mathbf D}^{-1/2},\quad \tilde{\mathbf A}=\mathbf A+\mathbf I,\quad \tilde D_{ii}=\sum_j\tilde A_{ij}.H(ℓ)=σ(A^H(ℓ−1)W(ℓ)),A^=D~−1/2A~D~−1/2,A~=A+I,D~ii​=j∑​A~ij​.

Node by node, with d~v=dv+1\tilde d_v=d_v+1d~v​=dv​+1,

hv(ℓ)=σ ⁣(∑u∈N(v)∪{v}1d~u d~v  W(ℓ)⊤hu(ℓ−1)).\boldsymbol{h}_v^{(\ell)}=\sigma\!\Big(\sum_{u\in\mathcal N(v)\cup\{v\}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\tilde d_u\,\tilde d_v}}\;\mathbf W^{(\ell)\top}\boldsymbol{h}_u^{(\ell-1)}\Big).hv(ℓ)​=σ(u∈N(v)∪{v}∑​d~u​d~v​​1​W(ℓ)⊤hu(ℓ−1)​).

So GCN aggregates a weighted sum over the neighbours and the node itself, with weights 1/d~ud~v1/\sqrt{\tilde d_u\tilde d_v}1/d~u​d~v​​ that depend only on the degrees, and then applies one shared linear map and a nonlinearity. Three design choices need justification: why the self-loop, why this particular degree normalization, and where the formula comes from.

Intuition for the normalization

Plain sum aggregation AH\mathbf A\mathbf HAH has a scale problem: a node with 1000 neighbours receives a vector 1000 times larger than a node with 1 neighbour, so feature magnitude would track degree and training would be unstable. Mean aggregation D−1A\mathbf D^{-1}\mathbf AD−1A fixes the scale (every row sums to one) but is asymmetric and treats a hub's message as important as a leaf's. The symmetric form D−1/2AD−1/2\mathbf D^{-1/2}\mathbf A\mathbf D^{-1/2}D−1/2AD−1/2 down-weights messages from high-degree nodes and to high-degree nodes: the pair (u,v)(u,v)(u,v) gets weight 1/dudv1/\sqrt{d_ud_v}1/du​dv​​. It also has a clean spectral meaning, derived next. The self-loop (+I+\mathbf I+I) lets a node retain its own signal. Without it a node's new state would be built only from its neighbours and its own features would be lost after a single layer.

Spectral motivation

From spectral graph convolution to the GCN layer

Step 1: graph Fourier transform. Take the eigendecomposition Lsym=UΛU⊤\mathbf L_{\mathrm{sym}}=\mathbf U\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf U^\topLsym​=UΛU⊤. The columns of U\mathbf UU play the role of Fourier modes. The graph Fourier transform of a signal x∈Rn\boldsymbol{x}\in\R^nx∈Rn is U⊤x\mathbf U^\top\boldsymbol{x}U⊤x.

Step 2: spectral filtering. On a regular grid, convolution is pointwise multiplication in the Fourier domain. By analogy, filter a signal by scaling each frequency component with a learned function gθg_\thetagθ​ of the eigenvalue: y=U gθ(Λ) U⊤x.\boldsymbol{y}=\mathbf U\,g_\theta(\boldsymbol\Lambda)\,\mathbf U^\top\boldsymbol{x}.y=Ugθ​(Λ)U⊤x. Computing this needs the full eigendecomposition (O(n3)O(n^3)O(n3)), produces filters that are not localized in space, and has nnn free parameters.

Step 3: polynomial filters. Parametrize gθg_\thetagθ​ as a degree-KKK polynomial in Λ\boldsymbol\LambdaΛ (Defferrard et al. 2016 use Chebyshev polynomials for numerical stability). Because UΛkU⊤=Lsymk\mathbf U\boldsymbol\Lambda^k\mathbf U^\top=\mathbf L_{\mathrm{sym}}^kUΛkU⊤=Lsymk​, U(∑k=0KθkΛk)U⊤x=∑k=0Kθk Lsymkx.\mathbf U\Big(\sum_{k=0}^K\theta_k\boldsymbol\Lambda^k\Big)\mathbf U^\top\boldsymbol{x}=\sum_{k=0}^K\theta_k\,\mathbf L_{\mathrm{sym}}^k\boldsymbol{x}.U(k=0∑K​θk​Λk)U⊤x=k=0∑K​θk​Lsymk​x. No eigendecomposition is needed, and since (Lk)ij=0(\mathbf L^k)_{ij}=0(Lk)ij​=0 whenever the distance between iii and jjj exceeds kkk, the filter is KKK-localized: it only mixes nodes within KKK hops.

Step 4: first order, one parameter. Kipf and Welling take K=1K=1K=1, approximate the largest eigenvalue λmax⁡≈2\lambda_{\max}\approx2λmax​≈2 and tie the two coefficients, θ=θ0=−θ1\theta=\theta_0=-\theta_1θ=θ0​=−θ1​. Using Lsym−I=−D−1/2AD−1/2\mathbf L_{\mathrm{sym}}-\mathbf I=-\mathbf D^{-1/2}\mathbf A\mathbf D^{-1/2}Lsym​−I=−D−1/2AD−1/2 this yields y≈θ(I+D−1/2AD−1/2)x.\boldsymbol{y}\approx\theta\big(\mathbf I+\mathbf D^{-1/2}\mathbf A\mathbf D^{-1/2}\big)\boldsymbol{x}.y≈θ(I+D−1/2AD−1/2)x.

Step 5: renormalization trick. The operator I+D−1/2AD−1/2\mathbf I+\mathbf D^{-1/2}\mathbf A\mathbf D^{-1/2}I+D−1/2AD−1/2 has eigenvalues in [0,2][0,2][0,2]. Stacking many layers repeatedly multiplies by something whose spectrum reaches 222, which makes activations explode or vanish. Replace it by I+D−1/2AD−1/2 ⟶ D~−1/2(A+I)D~−1/2=A^,\mathbf I+\mathbf D^{-1/2}\mathbf A\mathbf D^{-1/2}\ \longrightarrow\ \tilde{\mathbf D}^{-1/2}(\mathbf A+\mathbf I)\tilde{\mathbf D}^{-1/2}=\hat{\mathbf A},I+D−1/2AD−1/2 ⟶ D~−1/2(A+I)D~−1/2=A^, whose eigenvalues lie in (−1,1](-1,1](−1,1], with the largest equal to 111. Generalizing from a signal x\boldsymbol{x}x to a feature matrix H\mathbf HH with dind_{\mathrm{in}}din​ channels and doutd_{\mathrm{out}}dout​ filters (θ\thetaθ becomes a matrix W\mathbf WW) gives the GCN layer A^HW\hat{\mathbf A}\mathbf H\mathbf WA^HW.

The spectral picture explains what GCN does. The operator A^\hat{\mathbf A}A^ acts on a graph Laplacian eigenvector with eigenvalue λ\lambdaλ roughly as multiplication by 1−λ1-\lambda1−λ (exactly so for the version without self-loops, D−1/2AD−1/2=I−Lsym\mathbf D^{-1/2}\mathbf A\mathbf D^{-1/2}=\mathbf I-\mathbf L_{\mathrm{sym}}D−1/2AD−1/2=I−Lsym​). A smooth signal (λ≈0\lambda\approx0λ≈0) passes unchanged, a signal with λ≈1\lambda\approx1λ≈1 is annihilated, and a very oscillatory signal (λ≈2\lambda\approx2λ≈2) is passed with its sign flipped. GCN is a low-pass filter: it smooths node features over the graph. This is exactly what you want when neighbouring nodes tend to share labels (homophily), as in citation networks, and exactly wrong when they do not (heterophily), a limitation we return to in the pitfalls.

The even-KKK curves show a subtlety. Without self-loops, D−1/2AD−1/2\mathbf D^{-1/2}\mathbf A\mathbf D^{-1/2}D−1/2AD−1/2 has eigenvalue −1-1−1 on bipartite graphs (the alternating signal at λ=2\lambda=2λ=2), and its even powers keep that component at full strength, so the layer is not a pure low-pass filter. Adding the self-loop shifts the spectrum of A^\hat{\mathbf A}A^ away from −1-1−1 (its most negative eigenvalues are pulled towards zero), which is one more reason the renormalized operator behaves as a low-pass filter in practice and why it is stable to stack.

GCN in code

The NumPy version is three lines. Note that the rows of A^\hat{\mathbf A}A^ do not sum to one (it is symmetric-normalized, not a random-walk matrix), but its largest eigenvalue is exactly one.

pythongcn_numpy.py
import numpy as np

def gcn_norm(A):
    """A_hat = D~^{-1/2} (A + I) D~^{-1/2} (Kipf & Welling renormalization trick)."""
    A_tilde = A + np.eye(len(A))
    d = A_tilde.sum(1)
    return A_tilde / np.sqrt(np.outer(d, d))

def gcn_layer(A_hat, H, W):
    return np.maximum(0, A_hat @ H @ W)          # ReLU(A_hat H W)

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
A = np.zeros((6, 6))
for u, v in [(0, 1), (1, 2), (0, 2), (3, 4), (4, 5), (3, 5), (2, 3)]:
    A[u, v] = A[v, u] = 1.0
A_hat = gcn_norm(A)
print("row sums of A_hat (NOT 1 in general):", np.round(A_hat.sum(1), 3))
print("largest eigenvalue of A_hat:", np.round(np.linalg.eigvalsh(A_hat).max(), 6))

H0 = rng.normal(size=(6, 4)); W1 = rng.normal(size=(4, 8)) * 0.5; W2 = rng.normal(size=(8, 2)) * 0.5
H1 = gcn_layer(A_hat, H0, W1)
logits = A_hat @ H1 @ W2                          # second layer without ReLU -> logits
print(H1.shape, logits.shape)

largest eigenvalue of A_hat: 1.0
(6, 8) (6, 2)

In PyTorch you would write the same layer on an edge list so that memory scales with ∣E∣|E|∣E∣. The following module implements GCN from scratch with index_add_ as the scatter operation, which is a good way to see what PyG's GCNConv does internally.

pythongcn_torch.py
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class GCNLayer(nn.Module):
    """H' = A_hat H W on an edge list. edge_index: LongTensor [2, E] with (source, target)."""
    def __init__(self, d_in, d_out):
        super().__init__()
        self.lin = nn.Linear(d_in, d_out, bias=False)
        self.bias = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(d_out))

    def forward(self, x, edge_index):
        n = x.size(0)
        # add self loops (i -> i for every node)
        loops = torch.arange(n, device=x.device)
        src = torch.cat([edge_index[0], loops])
        dst = torch.cat([edge_index[1], loops])
        # degree of the target node in A + I (counts incoming edges incl. the loop)
        deg = torch.zeros(n, device=x.device).index_add_(0, dst, torch.ones_like(dst, dtype=torch.float))
        norm = deg[src].rsqrt() * deg[dst].rsqrt()          # 1 / sqrt(d_u d_v) per edge
        h = self.lin(x)                                      # [n, d_out], transform first (cheaper if d_out < d_in)
        out = torch.zeros_like(h).index_add_(0, dst, h[src] * norm.unsqueeze(1))   # scatter-add messages
        return out + self.bias

class GCN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_in, d_hidden, n_classes, p=0.5):
        super().__init__()
        self.l1, self.l2, self.p = GCNLayer(d_in, d_hidden), GCNLayer(d_hidden, n_classes), p

    def forward(self, x, edge_index):
        x = F.dropout(x, self.p, self.training)
        x = F.relu(self.l1(x, edge_index))
        x = F.dropout(x, self.p, self.training)
        return self.l2(x, edge_index)

# shape check on a random graph: 100 nodes, 500 random directed edges, 16 features, 3 classes
x = torch.randn(100, 16)
edge_index = torch.randint(0, 100, (2, 500))
print(GCN(16, 32, 3)(x, edge_index).shape)   # torch.Size([100, 3])

Two details worth noticing. The weights are applied before propagation (self.lin(x) then scatter) because A^(HW)=(A^H)W\hat{\mathbf A}(\mathbf H\mathbf W)=(\hat{\mathbf A}\mathbf H)\mathbf WA^(HW)=(A^H)W and it is cheaper to propagate the narrower matrix. And because the graph is fixed and the features of all nodes (including unlabeled ones) go through the network, the loss on the few labeled nodes backpropagates into the features of their unlabeled neighbours; this is how a labeled node "teaches" its neighbourhood.

Transductive versus inductive

GCN as trained by Kipf and Welling is transductive: the whole graph, including the test nodes (but not their labels), is present during training, and A^\hat{\mathbf A}A^ is computed once over it. A model is inductive if it can be applied to nodes or graphs not seen in training. The GCN layer has no dependence on nnn, so in principle it is inductive, but the full-batch recipe is not. GraphSAGE was designed around the inductive and large-graph use case.

GraphSAGE: sampling and separate self weights

GraphSAGE (Hamilton, Ying and Leskovec, 2017, NeurIPS, "Inductive representation learning on large graphs") addresses two practical limitations. Full-batch GCN needs the whole adjacency matrix in memory, and a hub node with 10610^6106 neighbours makes the cost of a single node unbounded. The remedies are neighbour sampling and an explicit separation between a node and its neighbourhood. One layer is

hv(ℓ)=σ(W1 hv(ℓ−1)+W2 AGG⁡({hu(ℓ−1):u∈S(v)})),\boldsymbol{h}_v^{(\ell)}=\sigma\Big(\mathbf W_1\,\boldsymbol{h}_v^{(\ell-1)}+\mathbf W_2\,\operatorname{AGG}\big(\{\boldsymbol{h}_u^{(\ell-1)}:u\in\mathcal S(v)\}\big)\Big),hv(ℓ)​=σ(W1​hv(ℓ−1)​+W2​AGG({hu(ℓ−1)​:u∈S(v)})),

(the original paper writes this as a concatenation [hv ∥ AGG⁡][\boldsymbol{h}_v\,\|\,\operatorname{AGG}][hv​∥AGG] followed by one matrix, which is equivalent to two matrices summed), where S(v)⊆N(v)\mathcal S(v)\subseteq\mathcal N(v)S(v)⊆N(v) is a fixed-size random sample of neighbours and AGG is a mean, a max-pool over per-neighbour MLP outputs, or an LSTM run over a random permutation of the sample (the LSTM is not permutation invariant, which the authors handle by random ordering). The embeddings are typically L2-normalized afterwards.

Sampling bounds the computation. If each layer samples sss neighbours, the computation tree of one node has at most sLs^LsL leaves regardless of the degrees, so mini-batches of target nodes have a predictable memory cost. At test time one can either sample again or use the full neighbourhood. Because the layer never refers to a global matrix, a trained model embeds nodes of a graph it has never seen (a new user, a new paper), which is the sense of inductive. Keeping W1\mathbf W_1W1​ separate from W2\mathbf W_2W2​ is also a real modeling improvement: a node's own features and its neighbourhood summary are different kinds of information, and the model can weight them differently (for example, when neighbours are noisy). GCN forces them through the same weights.

PinSage (Ying et al., 2018, KDD) scaled this recipe to a graph of three billion nodes at Pinterest, replacing uniform sampling by importance sampling from random walks.

Graph attention networks (GAT)

GCN weights every neighbour by a fixed function of the degrees. In many graphs some neighbours are more relevant than others, and the relevance depends on the features. Graph attention networks (Velickovic, Cucurull, Casanova, Romero, Lio and Bengio, 2018, ICLR) let the model learn the weights. This is the attention of Week 9 restricted to the graph neighbourhood: instead of attending over all tokens, node vvv attends over N(v)∪{v}\mathcal N(v)\cup\{v\}N(v)∪{v}.

First apply a shared linear map, zu=Whu\boldsymbol{z}_u=\mathbf W\boldsymbol{h}_uzu​=Whu​. For each edge (u→v)(u\to v)(u→v) compute an unnormalized score with a small learned vector a∈R2d′\boldsymbol{a}\in\R^{2d'}a∈R2d′ and a LeakyReLU,

evu=LeakyReLU⁡(a⊤[zv ∥ zu]),αvu=exp⁡(evu)∑k∈N(v)∪{v}exp⁡(evk),hv′=σ(∑u∈N(v)∪{v}αvu zu).e_{vu}=\operatorname{LeakyReLU}\big(\boldsymbol{a}^\top[\boldsymbol{z}_v\,\|\,\boldsymbol{z}_u]\big),\qquad \alpha_{vu}=\frac{\exp(e_{vu})}{\sum_{k\in\mathcal N(v)\cup\{v\}}\exp(e_{vk})},\qquad \boldsymbol{h}_v'=\sigma\Big(\sum_{u\in\mathcal N(v)\cup\{v\}}\alpha_{vu}\,\boldsymbol{z}_u\Big).evu​=LeakyReLU(a⊤[zv​∥zu​]),αvu​=∑k∈N(v)∪{v}​exp(evk​)exp(evu​)​,hv′​=σ(u∈N(v)∪{v}∑​αvu​zu​).

The softmax runs over the neighbours of vvv only, so the weights sum to one. As in Transformers, multi-head attention runs KKK independent copies and concatenates (hidden layers) or averages (final layer). Two remarks that are often misunderstood:

  • Static attention. Because the score is a1⊤zv+a2⊤zu\boldsymbol{a}_1^\top\boldsymbol{z}_v+\boldsymbol{a}_2^\top\boldsymbol{z}_ua1⊤​zv​+a2⊤​zu​ (the concatenation splits the dot product), the ranking of neighbours uuu is the same for every query node vvv, since only the a2⊤zu\boldsymbol{a}_2^\top\boldsymbol{z}_ua2⊤​zu​ term differs between neighbours. This was pointed out by Brody, Alon and Yahav (2022, "How attentive are graph attention networks?"), who proposed GATv2, evu=a⊤LeakyReLU⁡(W[hv∥hu])e_{vu}=\boldsymbol{a}^\top\operatorname{LeakyReLU}(\mathbf W[\boldsymbol{h}_v\|\boldsymbol{h}_u])evu​=a⊤LeakyReLU(W[hv​∥hu​]), which makes the ranking depend on the query ("dynamic attention").
  • Attention is still a convex combination. Weights are positive and sum to one, so a GAT neighbourhood summary is a weighted mean. It cannot count neighbours, which has consequences for expressive power below.
pythongat_torch.py
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class DenseGATLayer(nn.Module):
    """Multi-head GAT on a dense adjacency (clear but O(n^2); fine for n up to a few thousand)."""
    def __init__(self, d_in, d_out, heads=4, concat=True, neg_slope=0.2):
        super().__init__()
        self.h, self.d, self.concat = heads, d_out, concat
        self.W = nn.Linear(d_in, heads * d_out, bias=False)
        self.a_src = nn.Parameter(torch.empty(heads, d_out))   # acts on the neighbour u
        self.a_dst = nn.Parameter(torch.empty(heads, d_out))   # acts on the centre node v
        nn.init.xavier_uniform_(self.a_src); nn.init.xavier_uniform_(self.a_dst)
        self.neg_slope = neg_slope

    def forward(self, x, adj):
        # adj: [n, n] bool, adj[v, u] = True if u is a neighbour of v (include self loops!)
        n = x.size(0)
        z = self.W(x).view(n, self.h, self.d)                   # [n, H, d]
        s_dst = (z * self.a_dst).sum(-1)                        # [n, H]  score part for centre v
        s_src = (z * self.a_src).sum(-1)                        # [n, H]  score part for neighbour u
        e = F.leaky_relu(s_dst.unsqueeze(1) + s_src.unsqueeze(0), self.neg_slope)   # [n(v), n(u), H]
        e = e.masked_fill(~adj.unsqueeze(-1), float('-inf'))    # only real edges compete in the softmax
        alpha = torch.softmax(e, dim=1)                         # normalize over u for each v and head
        out = torch.einsum('vuh,uhd->vhd', alpha, z)            # weighted sum of neighbour features
        return out.reshape(n, -1) if self.concat else out.mean(1)

n = 5
adj = torch.eye(n, dtype=torch.bool); adj[0, 1] = adj[1, 0] = adj[1, 2] = adj[2, 1] = True
layer = DenseGATLayer(8, 16, heads=4)
print(layer(torch.randn(n, 8), adj).shape)                      # torch.Size([5, 64])

Forgetting the self-loops in adj leaves isolated nodes with a row of all −∞-\infty−∞ in the softmax, which produces nans. This is one of the most common ways a hand-written GAT crashes.

Graph isomorphism networks (GIN)

GCN, GraphSAGE-mean and GAT all aggregate with a mean-like operator. Xu, Hu, Leskovec and Jegelka (2019, ICLR, "How powerful are graph neural networks?") asked a sharper question: what is the most discriminative message-passing layer one can build? Their answer, the graph isomorphism network (GIN), is

hv(ℓ)=MLP⁡(ℓ)((1+ϵ(ℓ)) hv(ℓ−1)+∑u∈N(v)hu(ℓ−1)),\boldsymbol{h}_v^{(\ell)}=\operatorname{MLP}^{(\ell)}\Big((1+\epsilon^{(\ell)})\,\boldsymbol{h}_v^{(\ell-1)}+\sum_{u\in\mathcal N(v)}\boldsymbol{h}_u^{(\ell-1)}\Big),hv(ℓ)​=MLP(ℓ)((1+ϵ(ℓ))hv(ℓ−1)​+u∈N(v)∑​hu(ℓ−1)​),

with a learnable or fixed scalar ϵ\epsilonϵ (often 000). Two choices distinguish it: the aggregator is a plain sum and the transformation is a full MLP (at least one hidden layer) instead of one linear map. The reason is developed in the next section: sum over a multiset can be made injective, mean and max cannot, and an MLP is needed to approximate the injective function that realizes it.

Layer Aggregation weights Self handled by Sees degree? Typical use
GCN fixed, 1/d~ud~v1/\sqrt{\tilde d_u\tilde d_v}1/d~u​d~v​​ self-loop only through weights homophilous node classification, small graphs
GraphSAGE mean/max/LSTM over a sample separate W1\mathbf W_1W1​ no (mean) huge graphs, inductive, recommenders
GAT learned softmax αvu\alpha_{vu}αvu​ self-loop in the softmax no (convex combination) noisy neighbourhoods, edges of varying relevance
GIN sum (weights all 111) (1+ϵ)(1+\epsilon)(1+ϵ) term yes (sum counts) graph classification, chemistry

Sum aggregation is not free. It is scale-sensitive (large-degree nodes produce large activations), so in practice GIN is used with batch normalization inside the MLP, and on graphs with very heterogeneous degrees a mean can generalize better even though it is theoretically weaker. We now make "theoretically weaker" precise.

Expressive power and the Weisfeiler-Lehman test

Which graphs can a GNN tell apart? This matters because if two non-isomorphic graphs (say, two molecules with different properties) always receive the same embedding, no amount of training can separate them. Expressive power is about the limits of the architecture, not of optimization.

The 1-WL colour refinement algorithm

The 1-dimensional Weisfeiler-Lehman test (Weisfeiler and Leman, 1968), also called colour refinement or naive vertex classification, is a classical heuristic for graph isomorphism. It works as follows.

  1. Give every node an initial colour cv(0)c_v^{(0)}cv(0)​ (a constant if the graph has no node features, otherwise a hash of the features).
  2. Repeat: cv(t+1)=HASH⁡(cv(t), { ⁣ ⁣{cu(t):u∈N(v)} ⁣ ⁣})c_v^{(t+1)}=\operatorname{HASH}\big(c_v^{(t)},\ \{\!\!\{c_u^{(t)}:u\in\mathcal N(v)\}\!\!\}\big)cv(t+1)​=HASH(cv(t)​, {{cu(t)​:u∈N(v)}}), where HASH is any injective map from (colour, multiset of colours) to new colours.
  3. Stop when the partition of the nodes into colour classes no longer changes (at most nnn rounds).
  4. Compare the histograms of colours of the two graphs. If they differ at some round, the graphs are certainly non-isomorphic. If they agree forever, the test is inconclusive.

The test is one-sided: "different" is a proof; "same" is not. The message-passing equation above is exactly this procedure with neural networks in place of the hash. That is the whole connection, and Xu et al. and, independently, Morris et al. (2019, AAAI, "Weisfeiler and Leman go neural: higher-order graph neural networks") turned it into theorems.

The next demo runs colour refinement on two graphs simultaneously. Start with the hexagon versus two triangles, then try the pairs that 1-WL separates after one or two rounds, and observe the difference between "histograms differ" and "stable partition with equal histograms".

Interactive1-WL colour refinement on pairs of graphs
pythonwl.py
from collections import Counter

def wl_colors(adj, rounds=None, colors=None):
    """1-WL colour refinement. adj: list of neighbour lists. Returns the list of colour lists per round.
    Colours are canonical signature tuples (so they are comparable across graphs)."""
    n = len(adj)
    colors = colors or [0] * n
    history = [colors]
    for _ in range(rounds if rounds is not None else n):
        colors = [hash((colors[v], tuple(sorted(colors[u] for u in adj[v])))) for v in range(n)]
        history.append(colors)
    return history

def adj_from_edges(n, edges):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v in edges:
        adj[u].append(v); adj[v].append(u)
    return adj

hexagon = adj_from_edges(6, [(i, (i + 1) % 6) for i in range(6)])
triangles = adj_from_edges(6, [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 0), (3, 4), (4, 5), (5, 3)])
path = adj_from_edges(5, [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4)])
star_tail = adj_from_edges(5, [(0, 1), (0, 2), (0, 3), (3, 4)])

def wl_distinguishes(g1, g2, rounds=5):
    h1, h2 = wl_colors(g1, rounds), wl_colors(g2, rounds)
    return any(Counter(a) != Counter(b) for a, b in zip(h1, h2))

print("C6 vs 2xC3 distinguished:", wl_distinguishes(hexagon, triangles))
print("P5 vs tree distinguished:", wl_distinguishes(path, star_tail))
text
C6 vs 2xC3 distinguished: False
P5 vs tree distinguished: True

Precise statements

Multiset and injectivity

A function fff on multisets of node states is injective if two different multisets always give different outputs. A message-passing layer is at least as discriminative as 1-WL at a node if, whenever its two input states and neighbour multisets differ, its outputs differ.

Theorem 1 (upper bound; Xu et al. 2019, Morris et al. 2019). For any message-passing GNN with arbitrary (even learned) MESSAGE, AGGREGATE and UPDATE, if 1-WL assigns the same colour to two nodes after ttt rounds, then after ttt layers the GNN assigns them the same embedding. Consequently, if 1-WL does not distinguish two graphs, no such GNN with a permutation-invariant readout does either. Reason: by induction, embeddings are a function of the 1-WL colour. If the colours agree, the (state, multiset-of-neighbour-states) pairs agree, so the layer output agrees.

Theorem 2 (achievability; Xu et al. 2019). If the layers and the readout are injective on multisets of their inputs (for a countable feature space), the GNN distinguishes exactly the pairs of graphs that 1-WL distinguishes. GIN attains this: for a countable input space, Xu et al. show there exist fff and ϵ\epsilonϵ such that h(c,X)=(1+ϵ)f(c)+∑x∈Xf(x)h(c,X)=(1+\epsilon)f(c)+\sum_{x\in X}f(x)h(c,X)=(1+ϵ)f(c)+∑x∈X​f(x) is an injective function of the pair (c,X)(c,X)(c,X) of a state ccc and a finite multiset XXX, and an MLP can approximate the composition with the next transformation by the universal approximation theorem. Together: GIN is exactly as powerful as 1-WL, and no message-passing GNN is more powerful.

Why sum, and what mean and max lose

On multisets over a finite alphabet, sums distinguish more than the alternatives. Consider neighbour multisets of one-dimensional states:

Multiset sum mean max
{1,1,2,2}\{1,1,2,2\}{1,1,2,2} 6 1.5 2
{1,2}\{1,2\}{1,2} 3 1.5 2
{1,1,1,2}\{1,1,1,2\}{1,1,1,2} 5 1.25 2
{2,2}\{2,2\}{2,2} 4 2 2

Mean confuses {1,1,2,2}\{1,1,2,2\}{1,1,2,2} with {1,2}\{1,2\}{1,2}: it keeps the proportions (distribution) but loses multiplicities. Max confuses all four: it keeps only the set of distinct elements and discards both. Sum keeps the full multiset (given an injective embedding of each element, for instance one-hot encodings, the sum is the vector of counts). The hierarchy is therefore sum > mean > max in discriminative power, and the consequence is concrete: with identical node features, a mean-aggregation GNN cannot tell a node with two neighbours from a node with four, and a GAT (a weighted mean) inherits that limitation. A 6-node ring and a 12-node ring are indistinguishable to GCN-mean on constant features, while the degree is visible to GIN after a single layer.

Max and mean are not useless

The comparison is about distinguishing arbitrary multisets. In real data you often want the opposite: a statistic that is robust to the number of neighbours (mean), or that detects the presence of a rare feature (max). Corso et al. (2020, "Principal neighbourhood aggregation") combine several aggregators (mean, max, min, std) with degree-based scalers precisely because no single one is best.

What 1-WL cannot see

The hexagon and the two triangles in the figure are the canonical counterexample: both are 2-regular, so refinement starting from a constant colouring produces identical colourings forever. Any message-passing GNN therefore maps them to the same embedding, yet one is connected and the other is not, and one contains triangles and the other does not. This has practical consequences. Standard message-passing GNNs cannot detect triangles or count cycles in general (the two-triangle graph has them, the hexagon does not, and the embeddings are identical), and they cannot decide whether a graph is connected. For chemistry this matters because rings carry meaning: a well-known example is the pair decalin and bicyclopentyl, whose carbon skeletons are 1-WL-equivalent although one has two fused six-membered rings and the other two five-membered rings joined by a bond.

Ways to go beyond 1-WL, each with a cost:

  • Higher-order WL. The kkk-WL test colours kkk-tuples of nodes, and kkk-GNNs (Morris et al. 2019) mimic it. Cost grows like nkn^knk in memory, so k=2k=2k=2 or 333 is the practical limit. (There are two conventions in the literature, "folklore" and "oblivious" kkk-WL, which differ by one level of power, so check which one a paper uses.)
  • Structural and positional features. Add counts of triangles or cycles, random-walk return probabilities, or Laplacian eigenvectors to the node features. This breaks the symmetry between nodes that 1-WL treats alike, and it is cheap, but the features must be chosen well.
  • Random node features (Sato, Yamada and Kashima, 2021; Abboud et al., 2021): give each node a random label. This makes GNNs more expressive in a probabilistic sense, at the cost of variance and weaker generalization.
  • Subgraph GNNs that run message passing on many (rooted or node-deleted) subgraphs, and equivariant models with tensor features of higher order.

Expressivity is also not everything. 1-WL equivalence is a worst-case statement about distinguishability; real datasets rarely contain such adversarial pairs, and on many benchmarks a "weaker" GCN beats a "stronger" model because of optimization, generalization or over-smoothing. Treat WL power as a map of what is impossible, not as a predictor of accuracy.

Going deep: over-smoothing and over-squashing

CNNs got dramatically better with depth (ResNet had 152 layers; Week 6). Message-passing GNNs usually do not: the best Cora models have two layers, and accuracy typically drops beyond three or four. Two distinct phenomena explain this, and it is worth keeping them apart because they have different causes and different cures.

Over-smoothing

Over-smoothing is the tendency of node representations to become indistinguishable as depth grows. Intuition: every layer replaces a node's feature by an average of its neighbourhood. Averaging repeatedly is diffusion, and diffusion on a connected graph converges to a constant. After enough layers, a node in one community and a node in another hold nearly the same vector, and a classifier on top cannot separate them. Li, Han and Wu (2018, AAAI, "Deeper insights into graph convolutional networks for semi-supervised learning") observed that the GCN layer is a form of Laplacian smoothing and that repeated smoothing makes features of different classes converge.

Why repeated propagation converges

Take the linear part of KKK GCN layers, X(K)=A^KX\mathbf X^{(K)}=\hat{\mathbf A}^K\mathbf XX(K)=A^KX. The matrix A^\hat{\mathbf A}A^ is symmetric with eigenpairs (μi,ui)(\mu_i,\boldsymbol{u}_i)(μi​,ui​); for a connected graph with self-loops 1=μ1>μ2≥⋯≥μn>−11=\mu_1>\mu_2\ge\dots\ge\mu_n>-11=μ1​>μ2​≥⋯≥μn​>−1, and the top eigenvector is u1∝D~1/21\boldsymbol{u}_1\propto\tilde{\mathbf D}^{1/2}\boldsymbol{1}u1​∝D~1/21. Writing ci=ui⊤Xc_i=\boldsymbol{u}_i^\top\mathbf Xci​=ui⊤​X (a row vector of graph-Fourier coefficients), A^KX=∑i=1nμiK ui ci →K→∞ u1c1.\hat{\mathbf A}^K\mathbf X=\sum_{i=1}^n\mu_i^K\,\boldsymbol{u}_i\,\boldsymbol{c}_i\ \xrightarrow[K\to\infty]{}\ \boldsymbol{u}_1\boldsymbol{c}_1 .A^KX=i=1∑n​μiK​ui​ci​ K→∞​ u1​c1​. So every node ends up with the same direction c1\boldsymbol{c}_1c1​, scaled by d~v\sqrt{\tilde d_v}d~v​​: only the degree survives. The rate is governed by ρ=max⁡i≥2∣μi∣<1\rho=\max_{i\ge2}|\mu_i|<1ρ=maxi≥2​∣μi​∣<1 (the spectral gap).

To quantify it, define the degree-normalized Dirichlet energy E(X)=12∑i,jAij∥xid~i−xjd~j∥2=tr⁡(X⊤(I−A^)X)\mathcal E(\mathbf X)=\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}\big\|\tfrac{\boldsymbol{x}_i}{\sqrt{\tilde d_i}}-\tfrac{\boldsymbol{x}_j}{\sqrt{\tilde d_j}}\big\|^2=\operatorname{tr}\big(\mathbf X^\top(\mathbf I-\hat{\mathbf A})\mathbf X\big)E(X)=21​∑i,j​Aij​​d~i​​xi​​−d~j​​xj​​​2=tr(X⊤(I−A^)X). Then E(A^KX)=∑i≥1(1−μi) μi2K ∥ci∥2 ≤ ρ2K E(X),\mathcal E\big(\hat{\mathbf A}^K\mathbf X\big)=\sum_{i\ge1}(1-\mu_i)\,\mu_i^{2K}\,\|\boldsymbol{c}_i\|^2\ \le\ \rho^{2K}\,\mathcal E(\mathbf X),E(A^KX)=i≥1∑​(1−μi​)μi2K​∥ci​∥2 ≤ ρ2KE(X), because the i=1i=1i=1 term has 1−μ1=01-\mu_1=01−μ1​=0, and for i≥2i\ge2i≥2 we have μi2K≤ρ2K\mu_i^{2K}\le\rho^{2K}μi2K​≤ρ2K. Smoothness measured by energy therefore vanishes geometrically in the depth.

Oono and Suzuki (2020, ICLR) extended this to GCNs with ReLU and weight matrices: under conditions on the singular values of the weights, the features approach an invariant subspace exponentially fast, so deep GCNs lose the information needed for node classification. The following NumPy experiment measures the energy of a propagated feature matrix on a two-community random graph, and checks it against the prediction ρ2K\rho^{2K}ρ2K.

pythonoversmoothing.py
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# two-community random graph (stochastic block model), 200 nodes
n = 200
c = np.repeat([0, 1], n // 2)
P = np.where(c[:, None] == c[None, :], 0.08, 0.01)          # p_in = 0.08, p_out = 0.01
U = rng.random((n, n))
A = np.triu(U < P, 1); A = (A | A.T).astype(float)           # symmetric, no self loops

# node features: 2 weakly informative dims + 6 pure-noise dims
X0 = np.stack([(2 * c - 1) * 0.5, np.zeros(n)], 1) + rng.normal(size=(n, 2))
X0 = np.concatenate([X0, rng.normal(size=(n, 6))], 1)

A_tilde = A + np.eye(n)
d = A_tilde.sum(1)
S = A_tilde / np.sqrt(np.outer(d, d))                         # GCN propagation matrix
dn = 1 / np.sqrt(d)

def dirichlet_energy(X):
    """sum over edges of |x_i/sqrt(d_i) - x_j/sqrt(d_j)|^2 : degree-normalized roughness."""
    i, j = np.nonzero(np.triu(A, 1))
    return (((X[i] * dn[i, None] - X[j] * dn[j, None]) ** 2).sum())

def trajectory(alpha, K=32):
    X, E = X0.copy(), [dirichlet_energy(X0)]
    for _ in range(K):
        X = (1 - alpha) * S @ X + alpha * X0                  # alpha = 0: plain GCN propagation
        E.append(dirichlet_energy(X))
    return np.array(E) / E[0]

for alpha in (0.0, 0.1, 0.3):
    E = trajectory(alpha)
    print(f"alpha={alpha}:", {k: float(f"{E[k]:.3g}") for k in (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32)})

# the analytic prediction: energy decays like rho^(2k), rho = second-largest |eigenvalue| of S
mu = np.sort(np.abs(np.linalg.eigvalsh(S)))[::-1]
print("largest |eigenvalues| of S:", np.round(mu[:3], 4))

alpha=0.3: {1: 0.136, 2: 0.124, 4: 0.108, 8: 0.107, 16: 0.107, 32: 0.107}
largest |eigenvalues| of S: [1. 0.8643 0.6342]

With ρ=0.864\rho=0.864ρ=0.864 the late-time decay should be about ρ2K\rho^{2K}ρ2K: from K=16K=16K=16 to K=32K=32K=32 that is a factor 0.86432≈0.0090.864^{32}\approx0.0090.86432≈0.009, and the measured ratio 5.19×10−7/5.52×10−5≈0.00945.19\times10^{-7}/5.52\times10^{-5}\approx0.00945.19×10−7/5.52×10−5≈0.0094 agrees. The residual variants (α>0\alpha>0α>0, which mix the original features back in at each step) stop decaying and settle on a positive floor, because the fixed point of X=(1−α)A^X+αX0\mathbf X=(1-\alpha)\hat{\mathbf A}\mathbf X+\alpha\mathbf X_0X=(1−α)A^X+αX0​ is α(I−(1−α)A^)−1X0\alpha(\mathbf I-(1-\alpha)\hat{\mathbf A})^{-1}\mathbf X_0α(I−(1−α)A^)−1X0​, which is not constant.

The next demo makes the effect visible: a two-community graph with 2-D features, where you choose the number of layers and the strength of the residual link. Watch the two clouds slide together and the energy curve fall.

InteractiveOver-smoothing explorer: propagation depth and residual strength
Smoothing is not always bad, and depth is not the only cause

Smoothing is the purpose of a GCN layer: it averages out noise within a community. The problem is too much of it. Also, deep GNNs fail for reasons beyond smoothing: the vanishing-gradient and optimization problems of any deep network (there is no residual path by default), the entanglement of propagation and transformation (each layer both smooths and applies a weight matrix and nonlinearity), and over-squashing. Separating the propagation depth from the transformation depth, as in the APPNP and SGC models below, often recovers accuracy with many propagation steps and two weight matrices.

Over-squashing

Over-squashing (Alon and Yahav, 2021, ICLR, "On the bottleneck of graph neural networks and its practical implications") is a different failure: it is an information bottleneck, not a convergence. The rrr-hop neighbourhood of a node can contain a number of nodes that grows exponentially with rrr (on trees and on expander-like graphs), but the embedding hv(r)\boldsymbol{h}_v^{(r)}hv(r)​ has a fixed width ddd. All the information from those exponentially many nodes must be compressed into ddd numbers through the narrow edges on the way. Long-range dependencies therefore get crushed.

For a quantitative handle, Topping, Di Giovanni, Chamberlain, Dong and Bronstein (2022, ICLR, "Understanding over-squashing and bottlenecks on graphs via curvature") bound the sensitivity of a node's final embedding to another node's input through a Jacobian. If the message and update functions are Lipschitz with constants bounded by α\alphaα and β\betaβ, then for nodes u,vu,vu,v at distance rrr,

∥∂hv(r)∂xu∥ ≤ (αβ)r (A^r)vu(up to the exact normalization used).\left\|\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{h}_v^{(r)}}{\partial\boldsymbol{x}_u}\right\|\ \le\ (\alpha\beta)^r\,\big(\hat{\mathbf A}^r\big)_{vu}\quad(\text{up to the exact normalization used}).​∂xu​∂hv(r)​​​ ≤ (αβ)r(A^r)vu​(up to the exact normalization used).

The entry (A^r)vu(\hat{\mathbf A}^r)_{vu}(A^r)vu​ is the (normalized) number of length-rrr walks from vvv to uuu. When uuu is reachable only through a bottleneck (a bridge edge or a narrow cut) the entry is tiny, so the influence of uuu on vvv is provably small however the weights are trained. They linked this to negative Ollivier-Ricci curvature of the edges on the path: negatively curved edges are the bridges that squash. The two-triangle graph from the basics section is a miniature of this: the single bridge edge carries all information between the halves.

The growth of the receptive field is the reason bottlenecks bite on tree-like graphs and not on grids:

The tree curves are straight lines on the log axis: 3⋅2r−23\cdot2^r-23⋅2r−2 nodes at radius rrr for a 3-regular tree. A grid grows only quadratically, which is why long-range image tasks do not suffer over-squashing in the same way. Real molecular and social graphs lie in between, and the bottlenecks matter more than the raw counts.

Remedies for deep and long-range GNNs

The fixes fall into three families, matching the diagnoses.

Against over-smoothing: keep a path to the input and to the shallow features.

  • Residual connections (as in ResNet, Week 6): H(ℓ)=H(ℓ−1)+σ(A^H(ℓ−1)W)\mathbf H^{(\ell)}=\mathbf H^{(\ell-1)}+\sigma(\hat{\mathbf A}\mathbf H^{(\ell-1)}\mathbf W)H(ℓ)=H(ℓ−1)+σ(A^H(ℓ−1)W). DeepGCNs (Li et al., 2019, ICCV) combined residual and dense connections with dilated aggregation to train GNNs with over 50 layers.
  • Initial residual and identity mapping: GCNII (Chen et al., 2020, ICML) mixes the initial features H(0)\mathbf H^{(0)}H(0) into every layer, H(ℓ)=σ(((1−α)A^H(ℓ−1)+αH(0))((1−βℓ)I+βℓW(ℓ)))\mathbf H^{(\ell)}=\sigma\big(((1-\alpha)\hat{\mathbf A}\mathbf H^{(\ell-1)}+\alpha\mathbf H^{(0)})((1-\beta_\ell)\mathbf I+\beta_\ell\mathbf W^{(\ell)})\big)H(ℓ)=σ(((1−α)A^H(ℓ−1)+αH(0))((1−βℓ​)I+βℓ​W(ℓ))), and trains up to 64 layers. The α\alphaα term is exactly the residual used in the demo and the chart above.
  • Decoupling propagation from transformation: SGC (Wu et al., 2019) removes nonlinearities and computes A^KX\hat{\mathbf A}^K\mathbf XA^KX once, then fits logistic regression. APPNP (Klicpera, Bojchevski and Guennemann, 2019, ICLR, "Predict then propagate") first predicts with an MLP and then propagates the predictions with personalized PageRank, Z(k+1)=(1−α)A^Z(k)+αZ(0)\mathbf Z^{(k+1)}=(1-\alpha)\hat{\mathbf A}\mathbf Z^{(k)}+\alpha\mathbf Z^{(0)}Z(k+1)=(1−α)A^Z(k)+αZ(0), which is the same fixed-point-with-restart recursion as above.
  • Jumping knowledge (Xu et al., 2018, ICML): concatenate or max-pool the representations from all layers so the classifier can choose the depth for each node.
  • Normalization and regularization: PairNorm (Zhao and Akoglu, 2020, ICLR) re-centres and rescales features after each layer so that the total pairwise distance stays constant; DropEdge (Rong et al., 2020, ICLR) randomly removes edges during training, which slows the rate of smoothing and acts as augmentation; ordinary BatchNorm, LayerNorm and dropout also help optimization.

Against over-squashing: change the graph, not the weights.

  • Rewiring: add edges that shortcut bottlenecks. DIGL (Gasteiger, Weissenberger and Guennemann, 2019) replaces the adjacency by a sparsified personalized-PageRank diffusion; SDRF (Topping et al., 2022) adds edges around the most negatively curved ones and removes edges at the most positively curved; FoSR (Karhadkar, Banerjee and Montufar, 2023) adds edges that increase the spectral gap.
  • Virtual nodes: add one extra node connected to every node (Gilmer et al., 2017). It gives any two nodes a path of length 2 and carries global context, at the price of a bottleneck of its own.
  • Global attention: graph Transformers (below) connect every node pair in a single layer, trading structural bias and O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) cost for long-range mixing.
  • Wider hidden dimensions help in theory (Di Giovanni et al., 2023, ICML, "On over-squashing in message passing neural networks") but do not remove the topological bottleneck.
Rewiring is a trade-off

Adding edges mixes in information from nodes that were never connected in the data. On homophilous graphs this may hurt; on a molecule it changes the chemistry. Rewiring is a hyperparameter to validate, not a free lunch, and over-squashing and over-smoothing pull in opposite directions: shortcuts reduce squashing but speed up smoothing.

Pooling and readout

For graph-level prediction we need a single vector hG\boldsymbol{h}_GhG​ from the nnn node embeddings H∈Rn×d\mathbf H\in\R^{n\times d}H∈Rn×d, where nnn varies from graph to graph. The readout must be permutation invariant and handle any nnn. This is the same problem as DeepSets (Zaheer et al., 2017, NeurIPS), whose theorem says that a function on a set is invariant if and only if it can be written as ρ(∑vϕ(xv))\rho\big(\sum_{v}\phi(\boldsymbol{x}_v)\big)ρ(∑v​ϕ(xv​)) for suitable ϕ,ρ\phi,\rhoϕ,ρ (for countable inputs, and under suitable conditions). That is exactly "per-node transformation, sum, then an MLP".

Flat readouts.

  • Sum: hG=∑vhv\boldsymbol{h}_G=\sum_v\boldsymbol{h}_vhG​=∑v​hv​. It counts: a graph with twice as many identical nodes has twice the output. This is the right choice for extensive properties such as molecular energy or number of rings, and it is what GIN uses (with the sum taken at every layer and the results concatenated).
  • Mean: 1n∑vhv\frac1n\sum_v\boldsymbol{h}_vn1​∑v​hv​. Invariant to graph size, so better for intensive properties (a ratio, a type), but it cannot tell a graph from two disjoint copies of itself.
  • Max: element-wise maximum over nodes. It detects whether a pattern occurs anywhere, and ignores how often.
  • Attention / Set2Set / gated readouts: a learned weighting of nodes. Set2Set (Vinyals, Bengio and Kudlur, 2016) runs an LSTM that repeatedly attends over the set; gated attention readouts (Li et al., 2016, Gated Graph Neural Networks) compute ∑vσ(g(hv))⊙f(hv)\sum_v\sigma(g(\boldsymbol{h}_v))\odot f(\boldsymbol{h}_v)∑v​σ(g(hv​))⊙f(hv​).

Hierarchical pooling. Flat readouts discard structure in one step. CNNs instead pool gradually, shrinking resolution while increasing receptive field, and several graph methods mimic that by coarsening the graph:

  • DiffPool (Ying et al., 2018, NeurIPS) learns a soft assignment matrix S(ℓ)∈Rnℓ×nℓ+1\mathbf S^{(\ell)}\in\R^{n_\ell\times n_{\ell+1}}S(ℓ)∈Rnℓ​×nℓ+1​ of nodes to clusters with a GNN and a softmax, then forms a coarse graph X′=S⊤H\mathbf X'=\mathbf S^\top\mathbf HX′=S⊤H, A′=S⊤AS\mathbf A'=\mathbf S^\top\mathbf A\mathbf SA′=S⊤AS. It is differentiable but needs a dense S\mathbf SS (memory O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2)) and auxiliary losses (link-prediction and entropy) to make assignments sensible.
  • Top-k / Graph U-Nets (Gao and Ji, 2019, ICML) and SAGPool (Lee, Lee and Kang, 2019) score each node with a learned projection and keep the top fraction kkk, together with the induced subgraph. It is sparse and cheap but may disconnect the graph and drops nodes outright.
  • MinCut pooling (Bianchi et al., 2020) and others learn clusterings with a relaxed normalized-cut objective.

An honest summary of the evidence: on many benchmarks, simple sum or mean readouts of a good GNN match or beat elaborate hierarchical pooling (Mesquita, Souza and Kaski, 2020, "Rethinking pooling in graph neural networks" report that random or local pooling often performs on par with learned pooling). Start simple, and try hierarchical pooling when graphs are large and have clear multiscale structure (proteins, large molecules, meshes).

pythonreadout.py
import torch

def readout(h, batch, num_graphs, kind="sum"):
    """h: [N_total, d] node embeddings of a *batch* of graphs concatenated along dim 0.
    batch: LongTensor [N_total] giving the graph index of every node (as in PyG's Batch.batch)."""
    d = h.size(1)
    if kind in ("sum", "mean"):
        out = torch.zeros(num_graphs, d).index_add_(0, batch, h)
        if kind == "mean":
            counts = torch.zeros(num_graphs).index_add_(0, batch, torch.ones(h.size(0)))
            out = out / counts.clamp(min=1).unsqueeze(1)
        return out
    if kind == "max":
        out = torch.full((num_graphs, d), float("-inf"))
        return out.scatter_reduce(0, batch.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, d), h, reduce="amax", include_self=True)
    raise ValueError(kind)

# two graphs with 3 and 2 nodes -> one concatenated batch of 5 nodes
h = torch.tensor([[1., 0.], [2., 1.], [3., 0.], [10., 5.], [20., 5.]])
batch = torch.tensor([0, 0, 0, 1, 1])
for kind in ("sum", "mean", "max"):
    print(kind, readout(h, batch, 2, kind).tolist())
text
sum [[6.0, 1.0], [30.0, 10.0]]
mean [[2.0, 0.3333333432292938], [15.0, 5.0]]
max [[3.0, 1.0], [20.0, 5.0]]

Notice how the batch of graphs is handled: PyG concatenates the node features of all graphs in a mini-batch along one axis and the adjacency matrices become one big block-diagonal matrix (no edges between graphs), with a batch vector recording which graph each node belongs to. Message passing then needs no changes, and the readout is a segment reduction over batch. This is more efficient than padding to a common size.

Tasks: node, link and graph prediction

Node classification (and regression)

The setup in the GCN paper is semi-supervised node classification on a single large graph: a few nodes have labels (for Cora, 20 per class, 140 in total out of 2,708 nodes), and the goal is to label the rest. The loss is cross-entropy computed on the labeled nodes only, L=−∑v∈Vtrainlog⁡pθ(yv∣A,X)v\mathcal L=-\sum_{v\in\mathcal V_{\mathrm{train}}}\log p_\theta(y_v\mid\mathbf A,\mathbf X)_vL=−∑v∈Vtrain​​logpθ​(yv​∣A,X)v​, while forward passes use the whole graph. The reason it works is the homophily assumption: connected nodes tend to share labels, so the label information of a few nodes can be diffused to their neighbourhoods. Compare with the bar chart below: an MLP that ignores the edges reaches roughly 55% on Cora, the GCN reaches about 81.5%. About 26 points come from the structure alone.

Two practical points about node classification. Splits: the standard Planetoid split (Yang, Cohen and Salakhutdinov, 2016) uses 20 labeled nodes per class for training, 500 for validation and 1,000 for test; results on it are sensitive to the split, and Shchur et al. (2018, "Pitfalls of graph neural network evaluation") showed that with random splits and tuned baselines the ranking of models changes considerably. Mini-batching: for graphs too large for full-batch training, sample the computation tree of each target node (GraphSAGE's neighbour sampling, or cluster-based sampling as in Cluster-GCN), so each step touches a bounded subgraph.

Link prediction

Link prediction asks whether an edge (u,v)(u,v)(u,v) exists (or will exist). The standard recipe is an encoder-decoder: a GNN encoder produces node embeddings hu\boldsymbol{h}_uhu​, and a decoder scores pairs, for example a dot product suv=hu⊤hvs_{uv}=\boldsymbol{h}_u^\top\boldsymbol{h}_vsuv​=hu⊤​hv​ or an MLP on [hu⊙hv][\boldsymbol{h}_u\odot\boldsymbol{h}_v][hu​⊙hv​]. The graph auto-encoder (GAE, Kipf and Welling, 2016) trains the encoder so that σ(hu⊤hv)\sigma(\boldsymbol{h}_u^\top\boldsymbol{h}_v)σ(hu⊤​hv​) reconstructs the adjacency matrix. Training needs negative examples, because only positive edges are observed. Sample node pairs uniformly at random as negatives (usually one to several per positive) and minimize binary cross-entropy, L=−∑(u,v)∈E+log⁡σ(suv)−∑(u,v)∈E−log⁡(1−σ(suv)).\mathcal L=-\sum_{(u,v)\in E^+}\log\sigma(s_{uv})-\sum_{(u,v)\in E^-}\log\big(1-\sigma(s_{uv})\big).L=−(u,v)∈E+∑​logσ(suv​)−(u,v)∈E−∑​log(1−σ(suv​)). Alternatively use a ranking loss such as BPR (Bayesian personalized ranking, common for recommenders), −log⁡σ(suv+−suv−)-\log\sigma(s_{uv^+}-s_{uv^-})−logσ(suv+​−suv−​).

The two classic leaks in link prediction

(1) Message-passing leakage: if the target edge (u,v)(u,v)(u,v) is in the graph used for message passing during training, the encoder can read the answer off the structure and the model collapses at test time. Hold edges out: split the edges into message-passing edges and supervision edges, and never supervise on edges you also propagate over (PyG's RandomLinkSplit handles this). (2) Negative sampling at evaluation: ranking one positive against randomly drawn easy negatives overstates quality; use harder negatives or full ranking metrics (Hits@K, MRR) as in OGB benchmarks.

A known limit: a GNN encoder cannot distinguish nodes with isomorphic neighbourhoods, so two different pairs (u,v)(u,v)(u,v) and (u,w)(u,w)(u,w) with v,wv,wv,w structurally equivalent receive the same score, even when one pair is far apart in the graph. SEAL (Zhang and Chen, 2018) fixes this by classifying the enclosing subgraph around each candidate pair, with labels that mark each node's distance to the two endpoints.

pythonlink_prediction.py
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class LinkPredictor(nn.Module):
    """Encoder = any GNN producing [n, d] embeddings; decoder = dot product or MLP over pairs."""
    def __init__(self, encoder, d, decoder="dot"):
        super().__init__()
        self.encoder, self.kind = encoder, decoder
        if decoder == "mlp":
            self.mlp = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, d), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(d, 1))

    def score(self, z, pairs):                    # pairs: [2, P] node ids
        zu, zv = z[pairs[0]], z[pairs[1]]
        return (zu * zv).sum(-1) if self.kind == "dot" else self.mlp(zu * zv).squeeze(-1)

    def loss(self, x, mp_edges, pos, neg):
        z = self.encoder(x, mp_edges)             # message passing ONLY over mp_edges (not over supervision edges)
        s = torch.cat([self.score(z, pos), self.score(z, neg)])
        y = torch.cat([torch.ones(pos.size(1)), torch.zeros(neg.size(1))])
        return F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(s, y)

def sample_negatives(num_nodes, num, device=None):
    """Uniform random pairs as negatives (may rarely hit a true edge; fine for large sparse graphs)."""
    return torch.randint(0, num_nodes, (2, num), device=device)

# usage sketch: GCN encoder from earlier in this page (reuse the GCN class with n_classes = embedding size)
# model = LinkPredictor(GCN(d_in, 64, 32), d=32)
# loss = model.loss(x, train_mp_edges, train_pos_edges, sample_negatives(n, train_pos_edges.size(1)))

Graph classification and regression

Here each graph is a data point. The pipeline is message passing, then readout, then an MLP head: y^=MLP⁡(READOUT⁡({hv(L)}))\hat y=\operatorname{MLP}(\operatorname{READOUT}(\{\boldsymbol{h}_v^{(L)}\}))y^​=MLP(READOUT({hv(L)​})). Datasets are collections of many small graphs: the TU benchmark collection (MUTAG with 188 molecules labeled by mutagenicity, PROTEINS, ENZYMES, social datasets such as IMDB-B), and molecular benchmarks (ZINC, QM9 for quantum properties, the MoleculeNet and OGB-mol datasets). Standard practice, learned the hard way: TU datasets are tiny and noisy, so report 10-fold cross-validation with a fixed protocol (Errica et al., 2020, "A fair comparison of graph neural networks for graph classification" documented that inconsistent protocols had inflated many claims), and use a simple baseline (a tuned degree-and-feature MLP, or a WL kernel) next to any GNN.

Knowledge graphs and recommendation

For knowledge graphs the edges have types. R-GCN (Schlichtkrull et al., 2018) uses one weight matrix per relation, hv(ℓ)=σ(W0hv(ℓ−1)+∑r∈R∑u∈Nr(v)1cv,rWrhu(ℓ−1)),\boldsymbol{h}_v^{(\ell)}=\sigma\Big(\mathbf W_0\boldsymbol{h}_v^{(\ell-1)}+\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}\sum_{u\in\mathcal N_r(v)}\frac{1}{c_{v,r}}\mathbf W_r\boldsymbol{h}_u^{(\ell-1)}\Big),hv(ℓ)​=σ(W0​hv(ℓ−1)​+r∈R∑​u∈Nr​(v)∑​cv,r​1​Wr​hu(ℓ−1)​), with cv,rc_{v,r}cv,r​ a normalization such as ∣Nr(v)∣|\mathcal N_r(v)|∣Nr​(v)∣, and regularizes the Wr\mathbf W_rWr​ by basis decomposition (sharing a small set of bases across relations) to avoid parameter explosion with hundreds of relations. The classical non-GNN alternative, TransE (Bordes et al., 2013), embeds entities and relations so that h+r≈t\boldsymbol{h}+\boldsymbol{r}\approx\boldsymbol{t}h+r≈t for true triples; GNN encoders add the ability to use node features and neighbourhoods. For recommendation, treat users and items as the two sides of a bipartite graph. LightGCN (He et al., 2020, SIGIR) shows that for collaborative filtering without node features one should remove the feature transformations and nonlinearities of GCN: the embedding of a user is a weighted sum of embeddings propagated over KKK layers, E(k+1)=A^E(k)\mathbf E^{(k+1)}=\hat{\mathbf A}\mathbf E^{(k)}E(k+1)=A^E(k), with the final embedding the average over layers and a BPR loss on user-item pairs. It is a good reminder that more machinery is not always better when the input has no rich features.

Graph Transformers

Message passing is local. A Transformer (Week 9) lets every token attend to every other token in one layer, which removes both over-squashing (any two nodes are one hop apart) and the depth needed for long-range interactions. Applied naively to a graph, however, it treats nodes as a set and ignores the edges entirely: self-attention is permutation equivariant but knows nothing about who is connected to whom. A graph Transformer therefore has to inject the structure. There are three standard ways, usually combined.

  1. Positional and structural encodings on nodes. Append to each node feature a vector describing where it sits in the graph: the first kkk eigenvectors of the Laplacian (Dwivedi and Bresson, 2020; Kreuzer et al., 2021, "SAN"), random-walk return probabilities (RWSE), or degree and centrality. Laplacian eigenvectors generalize the sinusoidal position encodings of sequences: on a path graph they are exactly cosines.
  2. Attention bias from structure. Add a learned bias to the attention logits that depends on the relationship between the two nodes: shortest-path distance, or edge features along the shortest path. Graphormer (Ying et al., 2021, NeurIPS) uses centrality (degree) encodings on nodes, spatial (shortest-path distance) encodings and edge encodings as biases, and won the OGB large-scale quantum-chemistry challenge.
  3. Hybrid local plus global layers. GPS (Rampasek et al., 2022, NeurIPS, "Recipe for a general, powerful, scalable graph transformer") runs a message-passing layer and a global attention layer in parallel in each block and sums the outputs, with positional encodings fed in at the input. This keeps the local inductive bias that GNNs get cheaply, and adds global mixing.

Laplacian positional encodings come with an annoying ambiguity: if v\boldsymbol{v}v is an eigenvector then so is −v-\boldsymbol{v}−v, and if an eigenvalue is repeated, any rotation inside the eigenspace is also valid. A network should not depend on these arbitrary choices. Common practice is to flip signs randomly during training (data augmentation), or to use sign-invariant architectures (SignNet, Lim et al., 2023) that process v\boldsymbol{v}v and −v-\boldsymbol{v}−v identically.

pythonlaplacian_pe.py
import numpy as np

def laplacian_pe(A, k):
    """First k non-trivial eigenvectors of the symmetric normalized Laplacian as positional encodings."""
    deg = A.sum(1)
    L = np.eye(len(A)) - A / np.sqrt(np.outer(deg, deg))
    w, V = np.linalg.eigh(L)
    return V[:, 1:k + 1]                      # skip the trivial eigenvector (eigenvalue 0)

# path graph with 8 nodes: node 0 and node 7 are the far ends
n = 8
A = np.zeros((n, n))
for i in range(n - 1):
    A[i, i + 1] = A[i + 1, i] = 1
pe = laplacian_pe(A, 2)
print("PE shape:", pe.shape)
print("|pe(0)-pe(1)| =", np.round(np.linalg.norm(pe[0] - pe[1]), 3), "  |pe(0)-pe(7)| =", np.round(np.linalg.norm(pe[0] - pe[7]), 3))

# sign ambiguity: if v is an eigenvector then so is -v, so a model must not rely on the sign of a column
pe_flipped = pe * np.array([-1.0, 1.0])
print("raw PE identical after a sign flip:", np.allclose(pe, pe_flipped))
print("Gram matrix PE PE^T identical:     ", np.allclose(pe @ pe.T, pe_flipped @ pe_flipped.T))

# random-walk structural encoding: probability of returning to the start after k steps (k = 2, 4, 6, 8)
RW = A / A.sum(1, keepdims=True)
Pk, rwse = np.eye(n), []
for _ in range(8):
    Pk = Pk @ RW
    rwse.append(np.diag(Pk))
rwse = np.array(rwse).T                       # [n, 8]
print("RWSE of end node 0:     ", np.round(rwse[0, 1::2], 3))
print("RWSE of middle node 3:  ", np.round(rwse[3, 1::2], 3))
text
PE shape: (8, 2)
|pe(0)-pe(1)| = 0.113   |pe(0)-pe(7)| = 0.756
raw PE identical after a sign flip: False
Gram matrix PE PE^T identical: True
RWSE of end node 0:      [0.5   0.375 0.312 0.273]
RWSE of middle node 3:   [0.5   0.375 0.328 0.309]

Note how the RWSE of two nodes that look alike for a few steps starts to differ at k=6k=6k=6 (the middle node of a path sees both ends, the end node sees one), which is information a 1-hop aggregator cannot extract cheaply.

Do graph Transformers beat message passing? The evidence is mixed. They help on tasks with strong long-range interactions and on large molecular datasets with good encodings, and several analyses show that GNNs with tuned hyperparameters and virtual nodes are competitive on the long-range benchmarks (Tonshoff et al., 2023, "Where did the gap go? Reassessing the long-range graph benchmark"). The cost is O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) attention (mitigated by sparse or linear attention such as Exphormer), and without good encodings a graph Transformer is weaker than a GNN because it has lost the edges. Treat "global attention plus structure encodings" as one more tool, not a replacement.

Geometric deep learning: symmetry as a design principle

Step back from graphs. A CNN works because of translation symmetry: a cat shifted three pixels to the right is still a cat, and the same detector is useful at every position, so convolution shares weights across positions. A GNN works because of permutation symmetry: the same molecule with its atoms renumbered is the same molecule, so message passing treats every node identically and aggregates neighbours in an order-independent way.
